summary: The 1903 south-entrance light at Buffalo Harbor: a conical iron tower and fog-signal house, dark since 1993, owned by a preservation association since 2011.

light.characteristic: original lens: two white flashes and a red flash, each spaced ten seconds (LighthouseFriends); the station record's 'Fl R 2.5s' is not supported by these sources

access.note: LighthouseFriends: grounds open, tower closed; the lighthouse is inaccessible by land because of the surrounding industrial properties. USLHS place record: Open to Public: No; Active Aid to Navigation: No.

facts.agency: Buffalo Lighthouse Association (owner since 2011, per LighthouseFriends)

events.note: Act of 6 June 1900 appropriated $45,000 for the southern entrance lights
Two severe storms during the works damaged the breakwater and forced modified plans
Tower, fog-signal house and brick keepers' duplex built
Both south-entrance lights first exhibited 1 September 1903
Assistant keeper John Safe towed in a disabled airship
Air diaphone replaced the siren; station connected to commercial power by submarine cable
Radiobeacon established adjacent to the light, 4 April 1939
Automated; later replaced by a modern post light
Fourth-order lens removed; displayed at the Coast Guard's Buffalo station
Gallery optic active until 1993; a light on a nearby pole then took over
Deed transferred to the Buffalo Lighthouse Association
Fundraising for the first phase, a $185,000 stabilization and safety phase, began in 2012
Lens removed, restored and placed on display at the Heritage Discovery Center

corrections.proposed: confirm whether these are one light; if so, merge the two records
corrections.why: The USLHS place record (Buffalo South Breakwater, alternate name Buffalo Harbor Entrance South Side) and LighthouseFriends describe the same 1903 conical tower and fog-signal house under the two names. The 1912 pierhead light at the arm's end is a different light (LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The USLHS record and LighthouseFriends both give a fourth-order Fresnel lens for the 1903 light. No conflict remains on the order.

notes_for_editor: 1) Identity: the USLHS place 'Buffalo South Breakwater' (nid 3396, roster 36 lines) was matched by position (0.35 km) and part of the name, and its details (1903, conical, duplex, fog-signal building, discontinued 1993, alternate name Buffalo Harbor Entrance South Side) fit this light. Confirm the match. The sister record us-ny-buffalo-south-breakwater (pier_light, 1903-1993) may be the same light. 2) The 1912 'South Buffalo Pierhead Light' (flashing red acetylene, 43 ft, skeletal tower, at the end of the Stony Point arm) is a different light, per LighthouseFriends. The station record's 'Fl R 2.5s', focal height 12.2 m and range 4.3 nm are not supported by any source read here; LighthouseFriends describes the 1903 lens as a white-white-red group, and USLHS gives 43.5 ft above mean high water. Not corrected here. 3) Automation: LighthouseFriends says 1962. The English Wikipedia lead gives 1935 in its infobox; Wikipedia is a lead only and is not cited. Not reconciled. 4) The NRHP nomination (NRIS 07001191) is not digitised on NPGallery (the PDF is a 'not yet digitized' placeholder), and NARA's catalogue is not used. The NRHP listing year (2007 in the record) was not verified on a page read here. 5) LighthouseFriends' 1903 construction details (contract date, 2 October 1903 completion, Frank Petit's duplex, 1904 siren) cite Light-House Board reports for 1902-1904 that are not in the local corpus. They are footnoted to LighthouseFriends only. 6) Keepers: 36 roster lines from the USLHS place (roles normalised; USCG 1959-1962 lines kept as 'other'). 'John Safe' (USLHS) is 'John E. Safe' in LighthouseFriends; the 1915 Bulletin names John Safe as assistant keeper at this station, so the roster line is matched by station and role, not by name alone. No family relation among the Safes is stated in any source and none is claimed. 7) Chronicling America: a search for 'South Side light' with 'Safe' in New York papers, 1903-1920, returned no pages. Not pursued further. 8) The 1934 diaphone, the 1939 radiobeacon, the 1967 lens removal, the 1987 move and the 2013 restoration are from LighthouseFriends only. 9) Confidence medium: the primary sources cover the 1900-1901 plans and the 1915 rescue; most later history rests on LighthouseFriends. [Fact-check 2026-10-22] 10) Access: the earlier wording 'the sources do not say whether the tower is open' was wrong; LighthouseFriends says 'Grounds open, tower closed' and the USLHS record says 'Open to Public: No'. Corrected in facts.access. 11) The opening sentence now states the 1993 end of the gallery optic and that the light is inactive, instead of 'deactivated'. 12) LighthouseFriends prints 'Heritage Discover Center'; the story gives the place's name as 'Heritage Discovery Center'. 13) The 1915 rescue was read from the Bulletin page image (PDF page 39, printed p. 184): 'On September 13 John Safe, assistant keeper of South Buffalo South Side Light Station, etc., N.Y., towed to safety an airship.' 14) The 1901 storm passage was read from the scan text (scan page 217); the LHB 1900 passage from scan page 183. 15) The NPGallery asset page (NRIS 07001191, published 11/16/2007, 'Stony Pt. end of Buffalo Harbor S breakwater') confirms the listing and MPS group; the nomination PDF itself was not read.
